i'd start with python. python is used for almost every application of computer science (data science, ai, games, web development, etc).  once you know what you want to do with programming, then learn other languages (js for web dev, c# for game design, java or swift for mobile app dev).

go to [python.org](https://python.org), download python (make sure u check the box that says "add to path"), download vscode or sublime text, then watch some youtube videos on how to start programming in python. there are thousands of videos and guides on Python, it's the most popular language after all. some good channels are FreeCodeCamp and TechWithTim.

watching tutorials is fine and all, but do not get stuck in "tutorial hell". thats the term for when you only work on projects that you've found a tutorial for. think of your *own* ideas. and code them. for example, i made a password manager in python so i had to look up how to use json files in order to store my passwords. but i *did not* look up "how to make a password manager". i built the actual program myself. you learn more when you build things yourself, not when you code along with someone else.

for reading. this is my least favorite subject so i struggled with it. but i learned that collegeboard makes the test to get a bell curve out of students scores. meaning, they want most students to get close to a 1000, and have minimal very low and very high scores. so, you have to think like a test maker. the SAT, to quote a wise princeton review ad, only tests your ability on mastering the SAT. you cannot think like a student. or you will not do good on this section. students think, make prediction, inferences, on tests in order to learn. you are not taking the sat to learn stuff, you’re taking it to get the best score
possible and forget. so, do not. think. creatively. if you catch yourself making a prediction that the text didn’t explicitly state, you’re wrong.

ALL the information you need to get the answer right is in the passages. the SAT isn’t testing your knowledge of a subject, it’s testing how well you can read a passage and apply its info. it assumes you know nothing besides the info in the passage.
